column2: Start of the 1949 year (~45 students): return of M. C. Richards and Bill Levi, of Max Dehn full time, of David Corkran (history); Hazel Larsen (photography), the Jennerjahns (“Color,” “Modern Dance”), Joe Fiore (drawing, painting), Johanna Jalowetz; Quakers recruited: John McCandless (printing), Don Warrington (treasurer), Vollmer and Louise Hetherington (music), Robert C. Turner (ceramics, builds a kiln); Paul Leser and Flola Shepard from Olivet
Olson begins the Maximus Poems (ten already written when Williams decides to publish them)

Creeley, in Littleton (New Hampshire), fails to launch a magazine; through Cid Corman (the radio program “This Is Poetry,” Boston), he receives poems by Olson and replies that he seems to be “looking for a language”: the start of their correspondence, intense during Olson's stay in Yucatán (1950-51)

Two-day meeting at Stephen Forbes's: six former students (including Morton Steinau and Tasker Howard), Pittenger, and Corkran propose a Board of Overseers (choosing and removing the rector, salaries, budget, recruitment, fund-raising)

Stephen Forbes visits the college during the vacation: leans toward Levi's idea (adding five or six nonresidents to the Board); offers up to 6,000 dollars for a new science building; looks for a rector
Joel Oppenheimer at Black Mountain (1950-1953): painting, printing, poetry with M. C. Richards, relaxation exercises with Paul Goodman (summer 1950), then two years in Olson's workshop
Arrival of Joel Oppenheimer (age 20, dismissed from Cornell and the University of Chicago)

1950 summer session (eight weeks): Paul Goodman (writing), Clement Greenberg (art history and criticism), Theodoros Stamos (painting), Katherine Litz (dance), Leo Amino (sculpture), Robert Klein (theater)
“Homosexual summer”: student meetings on the “Goodman question” (a majority in favor); opposition from the Quakers and Dehn; Goodman accused of urinating behind a tree during a softball game

In the middle of a meeting, Ray Trayer hits Bill Levi (defense of Goodman, a remark about the farm); Joel Oppenheimer jumps on Trayer's back (“The Wild Bull of the Campus”); Johanna Jalowetz cheers him on
The faculty votes decisively against keeping Goodman for the year
Corkran decides to leave; with him, Trayer, the Quakers, and Goldowski give up (Goldowski marries an older student)
Corkran to Forbes (then March 27, 1951): “a situation to me personally repugnant and institutionally impossible”; departure of Corkran and the Quakers
Bill Levi leaves the community (his marriage is breaking up)
After Bill Levi's departure (December 1950), Mary Caroline Richards stays and makes the separation final; Wes Huss invites Levi to dinner with Natasha Goldowski before he leaves
Separation of Bill Levi and Mary Caroline Richards
Photos by Jonathan Williams: Charles Olson writing Maximus (1951); Francine du Plessix and Joel Oppenheimer (summer 1951)
Visit by Boris Aronson, stage designer, with his wife Lisa (the Jalowetzes' daughter): Olson's lectures “the most exciting thing you ever experienced”

Olson's writing workshop in the periodicals room of the Studies Building (smoke, cashmere sweater over his head): one must bring a text to get in; readings of texts sent by Creeley (“Mr. Blue”) or Duncan; diagrams of the “new sciences of man” (Mark Hedden's diary); Jack Rice's “Gothic seizure”; Paul Leser invited when African anthropology comes up

Departures in spring 1951: the Jennerjahns (France, GI Bill), Robert Turner (pottery in New York State), the Trayers (Earlham), Paul Leser (Hartford Seminary; resignation of April 24, 1951: “I am in love with [Black Mountain]”), Natasha Goldowski (a year in Paris)
Only two appointments accepted: Victor Sprague (biology) and John Adams (anthropology)
First issue of Cid Corman's Origin
Charles Olson comes back to settle at Black Mountain, from Lerma (Yucatán), with y & x and Call Me Ishmael; Ed Dorn prints A Letter for Melville on the college press

1951 summer session (~50 students, financially balanced): photography workshop (Hazel-Frieda Larsen, Harry Callahan, Arthur Siegel, Aaron Siskind); Katherine Litz; first stays of David Tudor and Lou Harrison; Ben Shahn (“Jolly Tales from the Hassidim”) and Robert Motherwell do not get along

The student Jay Watt's musical Flabbergasted, dances by Katherine Litz (including a dance inspired by Olson's Mayan glyphs); “Light-Sound-Movement Workshop”: a piece “after the Noh tradition” by Nick Cernovich

Francine du Plessix (Gray) spends the summers of 1951 and 1952 at Black Mountain, first for painting, then in Olson's writing class (Dostoevsky, Notes from Underground; the habit of keeping a diary; “Stop all this third person writing”)
David Tudor plays Boulez's Second Sonata; Olson: “the only piece of music since Bach”
Jonathan Williams in San Francisco (Rexroth, Duncan, Henry Miller): Jargon no. 1, a broadside of one of his poems engraved by David Ruff

Jonathan Williams at Black Mountain: Rolleiflex photography with Aaron Siskind, Olson's writing class one evening a week (one session from 7 to 11 p.m. continued at Ma Peak's tavern, then all night and the next day); two months of antagonism with Olson

The Black Mountain Review, vol. 1, no. 1 (the only issue), the college's magazine: ed. M. C. Richards, Joel Oppenheimer, Mary Fitton, Alex Kemeny, Hazel Larsen; a Noh play by Nick Cernovich, Goldowski on “High Speed Computing Machines,” poems by Russell Edson and Oppenheimer, “Father” by Fielding Dawson; a second issue typeset but never printed

Jargon nos. 2 to 4 printed at Black Mountain: no. 2 (a poem by Oppenheimer, a drawing by Rauschenberg, 150 copies, ~50 dollars), no. 3 (“Red/Gray,” six poems by Williams), no. 4 (poems by Victor Kalos, drawings by Dan Rice)
Winter 1952 enrollment: 35 students
John Cage's “mixed media” event

Olson's program of “institutes”: five eight-week institutes (crafts; theater — Boris Aronson approached; “new sciences of man” — Christopher Hawkes approached; natural sciences; the arts in summer); an inflated 1952-53 catalog (Goldowski, briefly back, nine courses; Huss eight; Sprague ten; Doyle Jones “Timber Operations”)
Ben Shahn, lecturing at the Philadelphia Museum, talks about Black Mountain; Michael Rumaker hears him

Jonathan Williams drafted into the army in January 1952 (two years, mostly in Stuttgart: Rainer Maria Gerhardt, the printer Cantz); an inheritance of 1,500 dollars from Charles Neal devoted to Olson's Maximus Poems

1952 summer session (~70 people): Charles Olson, Franz Kline, John Cage, Merce Cunningham, David Tudor, Robert Rauschenberg (back, married to Sue Weil), Stefan Wolpe and Hilda Morley (arrived at the start of the session); Katherine Litz
Stefan Wolpe replaces Lou Harrison (Guggenheim 1952-53) in composition; Hilda Morley teaches literature and Hebrew; Wolpe stays on after 1953 (Cage speaks of “usurpation”)
Cage announces a composition course in which the students would be his apprentices for the Williams Mix (funded by Paul and Vera Williams): no one enrolls; conversations and games of strip poker
Cunningham suffers from appendicitis (diet, ice pack); Olson perhaps takes his dance classes that summer (“like a light walrus”)
Karen Karnes and David Weinrib arrive as resident potters (80 dollars a month) in the studio built by Robert Turner; “potters-in-residence” outside the faculty the first year
Creeley already invited to teach in 1952 and announced in the summer session brochure (writing course)

Cage's “mixed media” event in the dining hall (Theatre Piece No. 1): Cage on a ladder or at a lectern (Zen, Meister Eckhart?), poems by Olson and M. C. Richards, paintings and phonograph by Rauschenberg, David Tudor at the prepared piano, Merce Cunningham dancing in the aisles chased by a dog, films and slides, coffee served in the white cups; until 10:30 p.m.; Stefan Wolpe walks out in protest; Johanna Jalowetz: “Deep in the middle ages”; Franz Kline in the audience
Cage's complete overnight reading of the Huang Po Doctrine of Universal Mind (20 to 30 listeners); readings of Artaud with David Tudor and M. C. Richards

“Institute of the New Sciences of Man”: a three-week seminar in archaeology and mythology with Olson, Robert Braidwood (Jarmo), and Marie-Louise von Franz (close to Jung); Christopher Hawkes does not come
End of the cattle herd: a dead cow, mastitis, manure, an escaped herd (Olson mooing in the pastures), auction at a time of falling prices
Disappointing tobacco crop; Jack Rice (Dan's brother) resigns after a quarrel with Huss (Olson carries a sign reading “I am exonerated”)
Death of Max Dehn from a heart attack shortly after the destruction of the dogwood forest; buried in the college woods
Michael Rumaker arrives on a work scholarship (like Ed Dorn): farm (silo), then kitchen seven days a week; he stays on and off for three years
Olson demolishes Rumaker's story about South Philadelphia in class; shortly afterward, “The Truck,” his first published story, is well received
Olson, at the last uncleared table: “I’m more important than any fucking dishwasher!”

The “reinvigorated” Community Council (about five months: dog droppings in the Studies Building, Fielding Dawson and the heating, Paul Goodman's dog Tinkerbelle looked after by Tim La Farge, recorders, students dressed as cowboys at the movies) resigns en bloc

At the end of 1953, Creeley agrees to edit a new Black Mountain Review from Majorca (“with Olson as mentor”); the college pays 400 to 500 dollars per issue (400-500 copies), printed in Spain by Mossén Alcovar
Arthur Penn begins directing for television

The Creeleys leave Aix-en-Provence (neighbors of Mitchell Goodman and Denise Levertov) for Majorca: Roebuck Press with Martin and Janet Seymour-Smith, then Divers Press (in 1954: Olson's Mayan Letters and In Cold Hell, in Thicket, Blackburn, Layton, Eigner, Duncan, Caesar’s Gate)
Jonathan Williams meets Creeley on a visit to Majorca

Last summer session: Esteban Vicente (painting), David Tudor (plays Beethoven to warm up, people come to listen), Merce Cunningham without Cage, with his company — Carolyn Brown, Viola Farber, Marianne Preger (Simon), Anita Dencks, Jo Anne Melsher, Remy Charlip, Paul Taylor; Franz Kline and Jack Tworkov; second ceramics institute (Karnes, Weinrib, Daniel Rhodes, Warren MacKenzie, Peter Voulkos)

Cunningham's six weeks: class in the morning, rehearsals in the afternoon and evening in the dining hall; Anita Dencks comes down with mumps after two weeks; beginning students (Harvey Lichtenstein, James Leo Herlihy — summer uncertain); Remy Charlip composes his first dance

Cunningham creates four dances — “Septet,” “Banjo” (Gottschalk, Tudor at the piano), “Dime a Dance” (Tudor), “Untitled Solo” (Christian Wolff) — and revives “Suite by Chance”; three performances for the community
Concert of Stefan Wolpe's music prepared by David Tudor

Switch to the quarter system; fees reduced from 1,600 to 850 dollars; the lower campus (dining hall–Studies Building) closed, then rented out: the end of twenty years of communal meals; budget estimated at 25,000 dollars a year
Fire that destroys Roadside

Resignations of Malrey Few (longtime cook), Flola Shepard, and Len Billing; end of the GI Bill; at the end of 1953, 24 students and no cash salaries for months; Johanna Jalowetz leaves to join her daughters after selling part of Jalowetz's collection (Schoenberg scores)
Winter 1954-55, the lowest point: a suicide attempt, a fire that destroys almost all of Joe Fiore's paintings, no money for coal; nine students and half a dozen teachers
Doyle Jones abruptly leaves the farm; two students take over from him; in 1955 the farm stops operating

Jonathan Williams, back from the army (family in Highlands), comes and goes at Black Mountain until 1956; publishes Anecdotes of the Late War and Olson's Maximus 11/22 (350 copies in 1956, 25 subscribers at 25 dollars)
Flola Shepard's departure: the end of all social engagement; two Black women students used to drive in from Asheville to take a few classes

Doyle Jones leaves the farm, cows sold; end of free food (hot plates, small refrigerators); cooking collectives at 2 dollars a week (Eric Weinberger); food stolen from the Black Mountain A&P; rotgut bought by Doyle at 5 dollars a gallon
Creeley arrives at Black Mountain at 8 in the morning after driving all night from New York in a 1940 pickup; Olson, naked in a towel, welcomes him and has him teach that very evening

Creeley's first class in the large lecture room of the Studies Building (six students, Karen Karnes asks him to speak up); then a small room: Hart Crane, W. C. Williams, Miles Davis, Charlie Parker, Bud Powell
Statement on “the situation of the College” to alumni, friends, and foundations (plans for “expansion,” an administrative secretary)

The Black Mountain Review no. 1 (64 pp.): Olson's “On First Looking Out of La Cosa’s Eyes” and “Against Wisdom As Such,” poems by Creeley, Blackburn, Layton, Eigner, eight reproductions of works by René Laubiès; contributing editors Blackburn, Layton, Olson, Rexroth (who withdraws because of Seymour-Smith's articles on Roethke and Dylan Thomas)
Forbes agrees to extend an overdue mortgage note (again in April 1955)
The Black Mountain Review no. 3: Duncan, “Letters for Denise Levertov: An A Muse Ment” (Levertov sees it as a parody, Olson as an attack); Creeley's note on Rexroth's withdrawal

Love triangle of Creeley, Dan Rice, and a student; Jargon publishes All That Is Lovely in Men (poems by Creeley, drawings by Dan Rice); Jargon no. 7: Creeley's The Immoral Proposition (drawings by Laubiès; 18 of 200 copies sold)
Creeley drinks in the afternoons at Ma Peak's tavern; Grey Stone comes to fetch him in a pickup on class evenings (“Now, teach”)

The college accepts a mentally disabled son of a wealthy Southerner, who is to announce his decision by flying over the college and waggling his wings; people watch for the plane for three or four days: it never comes
A man from the hills comes to provoke Olson (“the giant that walks the roads at night”): Olson breaks his jaw

Coming back from Ma Peak's tavern, Tom Field, needled by Creeley, drives the car into the chimney of a campus cottage (Rumaker on the steps): Field with a broken leg, Dan Rice his back (a brace for six months), Creeley a dislocated shoulder (15 dollars from the insurance)
Just before Christmas 1954, the community suspends all classes for three months; Creeley already gone (back in the summer); half the group leaves; 8 to 10 people remain; rumor of a permanent closing
Photos by Jonathan Williams: Robert Creeley (“Portrait as a Spanish Assassin”), Dan Rice and Creeley
During the suspension, a fund-raising tour of former supporters; Nell Rice's mission to Stephen Forbes leads to foreclosure proceedings
Don Mixon arrives as a student
Olson separates from Connie: he has a son (Charles Peter) with the student Betty Kaiser
Karen Karnes and David Weinrib join Paul Williams's Stony Point colony (Rockland County), where Cage, Cunningham, M. C. Richards, and David Tudor will come
Robert Duncan's first stay at Black Mountain
Nell Rice, Hazel Larsen, and Natasha Goldowski write to the nineteen former faculty members owed back pay, proposing a lawsuit; most refuse
Nell Rice goes on “permanent leave”

Robert Hellman (“The Quay,” BMR no. 1) teaches languages for about six months from summer 1955; Tony Landreau (weaving, a pupil of Dorothy Liebes) gets the looms in the Studies Building basement working again; brief visit by Martin Sprengling (Oriental Institute)
The Black Mountain Review, summer 1955: James Purdy's “Sound of Talking,” perhaps his first American publication

Michael Rumaker “graduates”: Olson's program (the Greeks, Shakespeare, the novel), Robert Duncan as outside examiner; a party and a diploma calligraphed by Joe Fiore (accepted in 1968 by the New School and Columbia)

Olson's course becomes “The Present” (prior reading of the New York Times and the Asheville Citizen-Times); Duncan teaches, including a course in Persian history; Dan Rice learns the trumpet and Spanish (from John and Elaine Chamberlain)
The sculptor John Chamberlain, from Chicago, spends a year at Black Mountain (“some great banal boy scout scene”); his work takes off
John Kasper (publisher of Pound's Square Dollar Series, later a segregationist of the White Citizens’ Councils) stays for two weeks
Enrollment rises from 9 to 12, then about 15 students in the winter and spring 1956 sessions
Fiore accuses Dan Rice of taking advantage of the college; Rice leaves; a few months later Fiore too talks of leaving
Olson's 1956 seminar reconstructed by Ann Charters (The Special View of History, 1970)

The case of a violent student in his thirties: his lawful wife, pregnant, complains to Travelers' Aid in Asheville; an investigation; risk of a morals charge (Olson not yet divorced); regular visits from the FBI
Photos of the farewell party for Hilda Morley and Stefan Wolpe; Betty Kaiser, Charles Olson, and Charles Peter, summer 1956 (Gerald van de Wiele)
Stefan Wolpe leaves the community for good in early 1956 (“couldn’t train professionals”)
